source_paper_text:
SOURCE: Olaf Parczyk and Christoph Spiegel, "Rainbow Schur triples: Things we
cannot do," The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 33(1) (2026), P1.45.
DOI: 10.37236/13554. Published 13 March 2026.
LICENSE: Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International
(CC BY-ND 4.0). The retained publisher PDF is unmodified.

The short source sentences below are transcribed with mathematical spacing
normalized. The epsilon statement is an explicitly labeled curator
formalization of the source's unnumbered tightness conjecture.

SOURCE DEFINITIONS (pages 1-2)

[n]={1,...,n}. A Schur triple is an ordered triple (x,y,z) in [n]^3 satisfying
x+y=z. The source counts (x,y,z) and (y,x,z) separately when x!=y. It therefore
counts exactly binom(n,2) ordered Schur triples in [n]. A triple is rainbow in
a 3-coloring when its three entries have three different colors.

SOURCE RESULT AND UNNUMBERED CONJECTURE (pages 1-2)

  Theorem 1. The maximum fraction of Schur triples that can be rainbow in a 3-coloring of the first n integers asymptotically is between 0.4 and 0.66364.

Immediately afterward, the authors write:

  We conjecture the lower bound to be tight and the underlying construction unique.

The tightness sentence is not numbered. The corrected canonical locator names
the paragraph after Theorem 1 rather than inventing a conjecture number.

EXACT EXECUTABLE FORMALIZATION

For every real epsilon>0, there is N such that, for every integer n>=N and
every coloring c:[n]->{1,2,3}, the number of rainbow ordered Schur triples is
at most (2/5+epsilon) binom(n,2).

This is exactly the upper-bound consequence of saying that the exhibited 0.4
lower bound is asymptotically tight. The target does not ask for uniqueness of
the extremal construction. Reversing the asymptotic quantifiers, counting
unordered triples, or proving only the existing 0.66364 bound is partial.
target: Prove the exact epsilon upper-bound formulation: for every epsilon > 0, for all sufficiently large positive integers n, every 3-coloring c:[n] -> {1,2,3} has at most (2/5+epsilon) times binom(n,2) rainbow ordered Schur triples (x,y,z) in [n]^3 satisfying x+y=z; or give and rigorously verify a counterexample sequence. A triple is rainbow when c(x), c(y), and c(z) are all different, and (x,y,z) and (y,x,z) count as different ordered triples when x != y.
title: Asymptotic two-fifths upper bound for rainbow Schur triples
